summary: Benioff argues the SaaS re-rating is cyclical, not structural: Salesforce has strong fundamentals ($46B revenue, $16B+ cash flow), is executing a massive $50B buyback, and AI tooling is making its products more efficient and capable than ever — positioning it well for the next cycle.
quote: we'll do over $46 billion this year, more than $16 billion in cash flow... we want to buy back as much as we can... Everything's going to be cheaper to make. It's more efficient. I can do things that I just could not do before.

summary: Chamath argues that high-end enterprise SaaS incumbents like Salesforce are well-positioned because AI is harder to deploy than expected, and the market will eventually rotate back to trusted platforms with strong C-suite relationships and proven net dollar retention.
quote: The high end of the market where Marc operates, where the large monoliths operate is quite safe... who has the best relationships, meaning they're inside the CXOs and the C-suite... Those guys I think are positioned to crush.

summary: Friedberg notes Salesforce is a platform he is actively investing in at his company, and sees a favorable arbitrage in horizontal enterprise software platforms versus vertical point solutions in the current AI environment.
quote: We're doing a big Salesforce implementation at Ohalo... we're doubling down our investment in horizontal tools... I think there's probably a good arbitrage there.

summary: Benioff notes HubSpot is trading at just 2x sales despite having a great recent quarter, reflecting the broader SaaS re-rating driven by AI fear rather than business fundamentals — implying the valuation is disconnected from underlying performance.
quote: HubSpot, they're trading at 2 times sales. I've never seen that before. They just had a great quarter... they're all trading at 2 times sales... there's like, you know, hypnosis around AI and we haven't seen it show up in the numbers yet.

summary: Benioff calls Anthropic a rocket ship, citing its focus on coding agents as the winning strategy, its $300M annual spend by Salesforce alone, and its transformative impact on enterprise software development.
quote: have you seen Anthropic? I mean, it is a rocket ship. That will not stop because you can use this product to do these incredible, amazing things... we are going to probably use $300 million of Anthropic this year at Salesforce coding.

summary: Benioff argues Anthropic won the AI race by focusing on coding agents while competitors chased other use cases, and its Claude 4.6 model created a step-change in enterprise coding productivity that has made it the dominant platform.

summary: Jason argues Apple has the clearest path to becoming a top AI player by leveraging its hardware footprint and running local models to maintain privacy, and explicitly names Apple as his top pick for the next year.
quote: Apple has the clearest path to becoming, you know, a top 2 or 3 player in AI simply by buying something like Perplexity or Mistral... I think Apple's my choice for the next year.

summary: Chamath is skeptical of Apple's local-model strategy, arguing that users need persistence across multiple devices and form factors, and questions whether Apple can pivot its decades-optimized organization if the hardware form factor changes entirely.
quote: I'm not a huge believer in these local models... you want persistence. You have multiple devices, multiple persona... the idea that you don't have persistence that follows you around in 2026, I think, is a breaking feature.

summary: Friedberg argues Google has a real opportunity to own the AI assistant interface by integrating Gemini deeply into its personal and enterprise data ecosystem (Gmail, Drive, Photos, G Suite), potentially making it a formidable competitor in the AI assistant market.

summary: Chamath argues the US should sell chips to China specifically to ensure NVIDIA wins the AI chip market over Huawei, framing continued NVIDIA dominance as the preferred strategic and commercial outcome.
quote: sell the chips. And the reason we should sell the chips is we want NVIDIA to win. We do not want to give enough oxygen for Huawei to then all of a sudden emerge and have a version of a chip that works. I'd rather he win than Huawei win.
